buildings.name: Forum Boarium
buildings.summary: The cattle market by the river landing, Rome's oldest trading place, between the Palatine, the Capitol and the Tiber: a cluster of the oldest cults (Hercules, Portunus, Fortuna, Mater Matuta) around the port, where Greek and Phoenician traders met Latins and Etruscans. A bronze bull from Aegina marked it.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) 162-164

buildings.note: Footprint is the present archaeological area around the two Republican temples; the ancient square extended further north and east.

buildings.name: Shrine of Portunus (archaic)
buildings.summary: The god of the harbour and of gates had his shrine (Portunium) by the river landing from early times; his festival, the Portunalia of 17 August, belongs to the oldest calendar.

buildings.name: Temple of Portunus
buildings.summary: The well-preserved Ionic temple by the river port, built about 100-80 BC: tetrastyle and pseudoperipteral, a porch two columns deep and a cella ringed by engaged half-columns, travertine for the free columns and corners and stuccoed tufa for the rest, on a podium 11.87 x 25.60 m. Restored in the 1st century AD; it became a church in 872, which saved it.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) 319

buildings.name: Round Temple of Hercules Victor (Olivarius)
buildings.summary: The oldest surviving marble building in Rome, built about 120 BC of Pentelic marble, probably by the Greek architect Hermodorus of Salamis for the oil merchant M. Octavius Herrenus, and dedicated to Hercules Victor (Olivarius, patron of the oil trade): a cella ringed by twenty Corinthian columns on a stepped base, 14.8 m across.

buildings.name: Ara Maxima of Hercules
buildings.summary: The Greatest Altar of Hercules Invictus, set up by Evander or by Hercules himself after killing Cacus, served until 312 BC by the Potitii and Pinarii; generals dedicated a tithe of their booty here. Coarelli identifies it with the massive tufa platform under Santa Maria in Cosmedin.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) 186-187

buildings.name: Ara Maxima of Hercules (rebuilt after 64)
buildings.summary: Listed by Tacitus among the venerable monuments burned in 64 and restored afterwards; dedications of urban praetors continue into the 3rd century.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) 187

buildings.name: Temple of Hercules Pompeianus
buildings.summary: Temple of Hercules near the Circus Maximus restored or rebuilt by Pompey, cited by Vitruvius with that of Ceres as an example of the widely spaced Tuscan (araeostyle) temple with terracotta and gilded bronze pediment figures.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) 188
buildings.note: Site near the Ara Maxima toward the Circus unknown.

buildings.name: Archaic temple at Sant Omobono
buildings.summary: The earliest known temple in Rome, a small Tuscan shrine of about 580-540 BC on a high podium with lavish terracottas including a Hercules and Minerva acroterial group; dismantled about 500 BC when the site was raised for the twin temples.

buildings.name: Arch of Janus (Quadrifrons)
buildings.summary: A four-way arch of marble-faced brick over a crossroads of the Velabrum at the edge of the Forum Boarium, with tiers of niches for statues; the 'arcus divi Constantini' of the Regionary catalogue, built for Constantine or his son Constantius II, perhaps as a shelter for the cattle traders.

buildings.name: Arch of the Argentarii
buildings.summary: A flat-lintelled marble gateway set up in 204 by the bankers and cattle dealers of the Forum Boarium for Septimius Severus, Julia Domna and their sons, with reliefs of sacrifice; Geta and Plautianus were erased from it.
